newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore Nov exports fall by unexpected 8.8 pct.
newsitem.headline: Singapore Nov exports fall by unexpected 8.8 pct.

text.p: Singapore's non-oil exports fell an unexpected 8.8 percent year-on-year in November to S$7.28 billion (US$5.20 billion), the Trade Development Board (TDB) said on Friday.
The previous month's figures had shown a small 1.1 percent rise and November's year-on-year fall stunned analysts who had predicted flat to slight growth.
"The whole market is shocked. The numbers suggest that in the short term domestic exports will remain weak," said Ng Bok Eng, regional economist with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Total exports declined less precipitously -- down 4.1 percent to S$14.87 billion -- as their fall was broken mainly by a 29.2 percent rise in the value of domestic oil exports thanks to higher oil prices and cold weather in Europe and the United States.
But the trade board offered little comfort on other fronts.
"Non-oil domestic exports remained volatile," it said in a statement.
Ng said the figures also "suggest no recovery in the key electronics sector yet".
Electronics, including disk drives and other computer-related products, account for more than 40 percent of Singapore's non-oil exports.
The industry worldwide is in a cyclical slowdown, mainly because of excess capacity in Singapore and other producer countries in Asia.
Song Seng Wun, regional economist with HG Asia, said the month-on-month data for disk drives and computer-related products showed the industry was still suffering.
He said recent reports of rising disk drive sales suggested increases could be "company specific" and not industrywide.
Song said it was also noteworthy that the figures showed the decline in domestic exports was across the board.
The trade board said non-oil domestic exports to key markets such as the United States, Europe, Malaysia, Japan and Hong Kong all declined in November.
Exports to the United States, Singapore's main trading partner, fell 2.7 percent to S$2 billion. Exports to Japan plummeted 14.3 percent to S$659 million.
Song said the sharp decline in November might lead him to adjust his fourth quarter gross domestic product (GDP) growth projection of a four percent rise.
"We still have to wait for the December figures. But it looks like manufacturing will remain anaemic. But the services side may pick up some slack," he said.
The recent World Trade Organisation conference which brought several thousand delegates into Singapore should boost the services sector in December, he added.
Ng said that while the short-term outlook remained weak for manufacturing, a recovery was expected especially in the second half of 1997.
